standard.title: Construct representations
standard.description: use media languages and media technologies to construct representations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can create arts works that communicate a recognisable idea and share them informally. They have explored media technologies through play. They have not yet deliberately applied media languages (shot types, composition) or production choices to construct representations with communicative intent.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use media languages and media technologies to construct representations that communicate identifiable ideas or stories.

nodes.label: Media languages — what they are and why they matter
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify at least two media language features (e.g. shot types: long, mid, close-up) and explain what each communicates to an audience.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify long-shot, mid-shot and close-up in an example media work and describe what each tells the audience about the story.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and describe a range of media language features in existing works (shot types, composition, sequencing, captions, voice-over); discuss what different choices communicate; use Viewpoints questions to frame observations.
wider: Investigate how shot type changes what the audience knows and feels about characters — comparing the same scene shot as a long-shot vs a close-up and discussing what is gained or lost
Explore how media languages in advertising (e.g. a camera-safety advertisement) differ from narrative storytelling — identifying the purpose and how language choices serve it
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding media language features (shot types, composition) is the conceptual foundation for all subsequent production decisions — without it, construction choices are arbitrary and cannot be evaluated or improved.

response_modes.reason: Students need explicit scaffolding to move from observing shot types to understanding why they communicate differently. Use structured questions: 'What does a close-up tell us that a long-shot doesn't?'

success_criteria: Student can identify at least two shot types (long, mid, close-up) in a media work
Student can explain what each shot type communicates to the audience

nodes.label: Constructing with media technologies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use a media technology to capture, sequence or edit media elements — making at least one deliberate compositional decision.
nodes.minimum_width: Use a digital device to capture and sequence at least three images or sounds, making at least one deliberate choice (which image to keep, how to order them, what caption to add).
nodes.typical_width: Capture and sequence images and text to create a media arts work (comic book, captioned sequence, voice-over story); select, edit and delete elements based on purpose; apply shot type decisions during capture; combine visual and audio elements.
wider: Explore claymation or simple animation by creating a character using images and/or sounds — making deliberate composition decisions at each stage and reflecting on what each choice communicates

Experiment with retelling a school day story using a digital camera to capture still or moving images and adding appropriate captions — reviewing and selecting the best images with Viewpoints questions: 'What images will I keep or delete?'

response_modes.reason: The mechanics of capture, sequencing and selection require practice — students who rush through production without deliberate selection and review produce accidental rather than intentional representations.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of production tasks available at Y1-2 (camera capture, voice-over, captioning, animation, comic) is genuinely diverse — students who work across multiple modalities develop much stronger production instincts.
success_criteria: Student uses a media technology to capture or create at least three media elements
Student makes at least one deliberate composition decision (selection, sequencing, or captioning) and can explain the reason for it

nodes.label: Representations communicate ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct a complete representation — a media arts work that communicates an identifiable story or idea to an audience.
nodes.minimum_width: Produce one media arts work (e.g. captioned image story, voice-over sequence, simple animation) that communicates a recognisable story or idea and present it to an audience.
nodes.typical_width: Produce media arts works across two or more forms for specific purposes (advertisement, story retelling, character creation); apply learned media language features (shot types, captions, sound) deliberately; reflect on whether the representation communicates the intended idea.
wider: Create an advertisement that recommends appropriate behaviour when using cameras — applying shot type decisions and discussing how the representation serves the persuasive purpose

Produce a media arts work that re-creates characters from a well-known story or song using selected and edited images, sound and text; reflect on how the re-creation communicates differently to the original

response_modes.reason: This node integrates media language knowledge with production skills — the work produced here is the evidence that both are operating together. Ensure students connect their language choices to their communicative intent.

success_criteria: Student produces a media arts work that communicates an identifiable story or idea
Student can describe at least one media language choice they made and why they made it
